summary: A chip-scale superconducting gravimeter couples a flux-tunable transmon qubit longitudinally to a nanomechanical beam via a parallel SQUID geometry, encoding gravitational acceleration as a geometric phase on the qubit. Stroboscopic readout at mechanical revival times suppresses entanglement-induced dephasing and achieves projected sensitivities of $6.5 	imes 10^{-9}$ to $6.7 	imes 10^{-10}$ m/s$^2$ with sub-millisecond interrogation.
motivation: Compact gravimeters face a trade-off between sensitivity and bandwidth; hybrid quantum architectures offer a path to miniaturization while maintaining precision, but existing chip-scale optomechanical and electromechanical devices lack the calibration and long-term stability needed for deployable gravimetric sensors.
method: The system Hamiltonian combines a transmon ($\Omega_q/2\pi = 6$ GHz, $E_C/h = 200$ MHz) longitudinally coupled ($g_0/2\pi \approx 18$–20 kHz) to a high-$Q_m$ nanomechanical beam ($\omega_m/2\pi = 100$ kHz, $m_\mathrm{eff} = 530$ ng, $Q_m = 10^9$ baseline; or 20 kHz, 10 μg, $Q_m = 10^{10}$ for high-mass design), with gravity-induced beam displacement modulating the mechanical SQUID flux and thus the qubit frequency via in-plane field $B = 100$ mT and lever arm $\ell = 50$ μm. Closed-form QFI and Cramér–Rao bounds are derived from the exact polaron-transformed evolution operator; realistic decoherence (qubit $T_1 = 0.8$ ms, $T_\phi = 1.5$ ms; readout fidelity $F_r = 0.995$) is incorporated via Lindblad master equation.
result: Near-term device achieves $6.5 \times 10^{-8}$ m/s$^2$/√Hz at $t^\star \approx 260$ μs (52 mechanical cycles), corresponding to $6.5 \times 10^{-9}$ m/s$^2$ absolute resolution over 600 s integration; high-mass design reaches $6.7 \times 10^{-9}$ m/s$^2$/√Hz at $t^\star \approx 250$ μs (10 cycles), or $6.7 \times 10^{-10}$ m/s$^2$ over 600 s, comparable to atom-interferometer precision with three orders of magnitude faster cycle times.
